Rising geopolitical conflict across the world is driving countries in multiple regions to establish new bilateral currency swap facilities. In the Middle East, the UAE has extended a new local-currency (dirham) swap line to Bahrain—whose debt has surged owing to a drop in oil revenues from Iran’s attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Russia—financially constrained by sharply curtailed access to the SWIFT global cross-border payments system since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine—has established a new swap line with Kazakhstan.

Since the financial crisis of 2007, central banks around the world have entered into a multitude of bilateral currency swap agreements with one another. These agreements allow a central bank in one country to exchange currency, usually its domestic currency, for a certain amount of foreign currency. The recipient central bank can then lend this foreign currency on to its domestic banks, on its own terms and at its own risk.

📝 New article on Our World in Data: How much development aid is spent on climate change?

For a long time, we didn’t have good data to answer this basic question. But using tags from the RioMarkers database, we’ve constructed a dataset on how much aid is spent on climate change, and what that funding is used for.

The headline result is that, in 2024, around one-fifth of development aid was climate-related. For allocable bilateral aid — that is, aid given from one country to another for specific projects — the share was one-third.

Some of that aid is given to climate mitigation projects, which aim to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Some is given to adaptation: ways of dealing with the impacts of climate change. And just as much is given to projects that do both.

Whether climate-related aid is in conflict or crowds out other aid efforts is hard to untangle. When we look at individual examples, many look like traditional aid projects, with a subtle link to climate efforts. Take the building of a hospital in Tanzania; its main objective is to provide healthcare and save lives. But it’s also tagged as a climate-related project because it was built with energy efficiency in mind. Would that hospital have been built in a world without climate change? Probably.

Other cases are less clear. Concerns about the displacement of traditional projects seem real, but so too are concerns that commitments to climate finance are often met through a relabeling exercise.

In our article, we dig into the data on climate-related aid projects: how it’s changed over time and which countries give and receive it.

ActionRAG: Evidence-Refining Graph Diffusion for Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents
Navyansh Mahlanavyansh@actioneer.comSashank Vandrangisashank@actioneer.comActioneer, Mountain View, California, USAAbstract
LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retroevaluation. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels and applies tiered entity resolution. Given a query, dual-channel entity and triple retrieval forms an initial evidence set and induces a bounded local graph. Query-conditioned receiver-normalized diffusion refines triple scores using local path structure. Seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization preserve direct evidence while recovering missed connections. We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), which tests accurate retrieval, conflict resolution, long-range understanding, and test-time learning. Across its eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG achieves 55.1 average accuracy, improving over the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points. Under MAB’s query-time cost accounting, mean synthesis cost stays below $0.001 per query on the four reported cost columns, and the sum of separately measured retrieval-side p99 components is 440.7 ms on our consumer Apple Silicon setup.volume: 353,year: 2026workshop: ACML 2026editors: Andy Song, Bo Han and Sarah Erfanigraph retrieval-augmented generation; graph diffusion filtering; memory-augmented LLM agents; knowledge graphskeywords

1Introduction
Large language model (LLM) agents accumulate information across many turns of interaction and must recall, reconcile, and update facts as those interactions unfold. A useful memory for such agents is not a single skill but a bundle of them: looking up a specific fact buried deep in past dialogue, reasoning across several facts to answer a multi-hop question, recognizing when a new statement supersedes an older one, and absorbing fresh information at test time. MemoryAgentBench (MAB) (Hu et al., 2026) operationalizes exactly this view, evaluating memory in LLM agents via incremental multi-turn interactions along four competencies: accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, and conflict resolution.The dominant memory architecture today is dense retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020): chunk the interaction history, embed each chunk, and look up the top-k matches per query. This flat index works for single-hop fact recall but loses signal on multi-hop reasoning (each chunk is scored in isolation) and on conflict resolution (a superseded fact and the fact that overrides it share most of their semantic content and become indistinguishable to a chunk embedder). The result is a measurable accuracy gap on exactly the MemoryAgentBench slices that real agents need to handle.Graph-structured memory addresses this by representing the agent’s history as a typed entity–relation graph. Microsoft’s GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) and LightRAG (Guo et al., 2024) use shallow heuristic traversal over the resulting graph, which is fast but loses much of the multi-hop signal. HippoRAG (Gutiérrez et al., 2024) and its successor HippoRAG-v2 (Gutiérrez et al., 2025) take the stronger route of extracting named entities from the query, linking them to nodes in a global corpus graph, and using those nodes to seed Personalized PageRank (PPR) (Page et al., 1999; Haveliwala, 2002). This provides effective associative retrieval, but it introduces an LLM call before every graph search and makes retrieval depend on the entities retained by that call. Predicate-level cues that are not expressed as salient named entities may therefore receive weak or no initial activation, causing relevant relations to be overlooked. ActionRAG instead retrieves both entity and concrete triple seeds directly, then uses local graph diffusion to retroevaluate the resulting triples. This removes query-time LLM parsing from retrieval while preserving relational cues that entity-only seeding can miss.Although an agent’s memory may be large, evidence relevant to a particular query often occupies a small region once plausible entities and relations have been identified. ActionRAG builds this region over a cautiously indexed entity–relation graph. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels, resolves repeated or ambiguous entities through tiered checks, and preserves source provenance. At query time, direct retrieval over both entities and concrete triples produces an initial evidence set. ActionRAG then constructs a bounded local graph and applies query-conditioned, receiver-normalized diffusion to revise triple relevance using surrounding path structure. Graph connectivity therefore acts as a second-stage evaluator of retrieved evidence rather than replacing semantic retrieval altogether. We evaluate ActionRAG on the eight deterministic-scoring columns of MemoryAgentBench. ActionRAG has the highest reported score among retrieval-based memory agents on six of the eight columns where the unweighted mean of these heterogeneous scores is 55.1, 5.4 points above HippoRAG-v2.Contributions.
•A cautious graph-indexing pipeline with label reconciliation, tiered entity resolution, provenance preservation, and conflict-aware summarization.
•An evidence-refining local graph diffusion method that combines dual-channel retrieval with relational retroevaluation, yielding the highest reported score among retrieval-based memory agents on six of the eight deterministic MAB columns.
2Related Work

2.1Long-Context and Memory-Augmented LLMs
One line of work expands the context window to hold an entire interaction history. Frontier models offer 128K–1M token contexts (OpenAI, 2024b; Anthropic, 2024; Gemini Team, Google, 2024), while position interpolation (Chen et al., 2023), NTK and YaRN scaling (Peng et al., 2024), and LongRoPE (Ding et al., 2024) extend them further. However, accuracy declines when relevant information lies deep in the window (Liu et al., 2024; Kamradt, 2023), and inference cost rises with context length, so long context alone is insufficient.External-memory systems instead store information around the LLM. MemGPT (Packer et al., 2024) pages between a small in-context working memory and a larger archive, a design productionised by Letta (Letta, 2024). Mem0 and Mem0g (Chhikara et al., 2025) extract structured user facts and retrieve them through a learned policy. A-MEM (Xu et al., 2025) adds agentic links and a self-organising memory graph and Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025) maintains a temporal knowledge graph for evolving facts. Agentic retrieval systems such as Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024) and MIRIX (Wang and Chen, 2025) add reflection or multi-agent memory control around retrieval. These systems address the competencies defined by MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2026): accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, and conflict resolution. Their retrieval can nevertheless depend on opaque learned policies or flat similarity lookups that underuse structural signal.
2.2Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020; Guu et al., 2020) conditions an LLM on top-k documents retrieved by a sparse model such as BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) or a dense bi-encoder (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Izacard et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2024). Recent embedding baselines include proprietary OpenAI Text-Embedding-3 models (OpenAI, 2024a) and Qwen3-Embedding (Zhang et al., 2025). Stronger pipelines add cross-encoder or LLM re-rankers (Nogueira et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2023), or late-interaction models such as ColBERT and ColBERTv2 (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020; Santhanam et al., 2022). On MemoryAgentBench, dense RAG is competitive for accurate retrieval but underperforms on multi-hop and conflict-resolution questions. Independent chunk scoring misses cross-chunk structure and cannot reliably distinguish semantically similar statements when one supersedes the other.
2.3Knowledge Graphs for Retrieval and Reasoning
A complementary line structures retrieval through graphs or persistent memory. RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024) builds a tree of recursive summaries, GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) extracts an entity–relation graph and summarises its communities for global queries, and LightRAG (Guo et al., 2024) combines local entity and global relation retrieval over a lightweight graph. Cognee (Markovic et al., 2025) optimises the interface between knowledge graphs and LLMs for multi-hop reasoning. These approaches can underrepresent specific relational paths through summarization or heuristic expansion. Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) extracts and consolidates salient conversational memories, and its graph variant represents entities and relations to support relational retrieval. A-MEM (Xu et al., 2025) organises memories as Zettelkasten-inspired notes with generated attributes and dynamic links, updating existing notes as new evidence arrives. MemoRAG (Qian et al., 2025) instead uses a dual-system architecture: a lightweight long-range model forms global memory and generates draft-answer clues that guide retrieval for a more expressive answering model.HippoRAG (Gutiérrez et al., 2024) seeds Personalized PageRank (Page et al., 1999; Haveliwala, 2002) over a corpus-level entity graph using query-relevant entities, then aggregates propagated scores to passages. HippoRAG-v2 (Gutiérrez et al., 2025) strengthens passage integration and the online use of an LLM. More broadly, graph diffusion propagates local relevance through weighted transition powers, with Personalized PageRank and heat kernels as common instances (Klicpera et al., 2019). Collectively, these methods span community summarization, dynamic memory linking, memory-guided clue generation, and global graph propagation, with trade-offs in query-time model calls, graph-wide computation, and dependence on preselected entity cues.

3.1Overview

3.2Cautious Graph Construction
The indexer turns an interaction history into an entity–relation graph and records the source chunk for every graph item. Chunks are processed in parallel, but names and types are resolved across the complete batch before the graph is updated.
Structured extraction and temporal grounding.
For each chunk, an LLM emits typed entity mentions and directed (head,relation,tail) mentions with textual descriptions. The current type vocabulary is supplied as a soft constraint, allowing the extractor to introduce a more specific label when no existing type is suitable. Dates, durations, and temporal phrases are retained inside the corresponding entity or relation description rather than represented as graph nodes. When a dialogue has a session timestamp, relative phrases such as “yesterday” or “last week” are converted to absolute dates using that timestamp. The resolved date is stored in the fact description instead of creating a separate node for it.
Label reconciliation.
Free-form extraction improves coverage but can produce several names for the same entity type. Before updating the graph, the indexer groups proposed types using name and description similarity, maps each group to an existing canonical type when possible, and registers unmatched groups as new types. Alias chains are resolved before the resulting type map is applied to the batch.
Entity resolution.
Mentions are resolved after their types have been canonicalized. A unique node with the same normalized name and a compatible type is reused directly. If no exact match exists, the indexer reuses a fuzzy name match only when it is the clear best candidate. All remaining mentions are grouped by normalized name, canonical type, and description similarity. One node is then created for each group before any relations are written, preventing parallel workers from creating duplicate nodes. Resolved entity pairs are stored as typed triples, with repeated observations merged into the same edge. Each graph item retains links to its source chunks, preserving the original evidence.
Temporal graph summarization.
Nodes and relations supported by several mentions are periodically summarized into a single description. Hierarchical summarization retains dates and links to the source chunks, after which the updated description is embedded for retrieval. The graph thus provides a compact semantic representation while the original evidence remains available through these links.
3.3Query-Time Evidence Refinement by Graph Diffusion

Motivation.
Semantic retrieval scores graph items independently. It can therefore retrieve two strongly matching facts while missing the relation that connects them, simply because the connecting relation is not itself similar to the query. Unrestricted graph expansion has the opposite problem: high-degree entities introduce many generic facts and consume the context budget. The evidence order is intentionally two stage: retained seed-supported items are packed first by diffused score, then materialized bridge triples are appended by flux. 4Experiments
We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2026), which tests long-term memory through incremental multi-turn interactions. We report its eight deterministic task columns across four competencies: accurate retrieval (SH-DocQA, MH-DocQA, and EventQA), conflict resolution (FC-SH and FC-MH), long-range understanding (Detective QA), and test-time learning (MCC and Recom). All ActionRAG results use the receiver-normalized diffusion method in Section 3.3; unless stated otherwise, all baseline numbers are taken directly from the MAB paper. We compare against the MAB baseline families most relevant to retrieval-based memory: long-context references, simple and embedding RAG, structure-augmented RAG, and agentic memory agents, including HippoRAG-v2 (Gutiérrez et al., 2025).
4.1Setup

Benchmark and scoring.
The eight columns aggregate finer-grained datasets: SH-DocQA and MH-DocQA from RULER, three context-length variants of EventQA, five in-context classification datasets for MCC, Redial for Recom, Detective QA, and four context-length variants each for FC-SH and FC-MH. Following MAB, we use substring exact match for DocQA, EventQA, and fact consolidation, exact match for MCC and Detective QA, and Recall@5 for Recom. We preserve MAB’s within-column aggregation and report the unweighted mean of the eight column scores as the “deterministic average.” Tasks requiring an LLM judge are excluded from this aggregate.
ActionRAG configuration.
Each query retrieves the ten nearest entities and ten nearest concrete triples. Entity seeds are expanded by at most two hops and triple seeds by one hop, after which the initial set is capped at 200 items. The query-local graph uses hop bound H=3, distance-decay rate β=1, and minimum traversal cost δ=0.01. We apply one receiver-normalized solve with direct-evidence weight α=0.15; no second diffusion round is performed. Items scoring below ε=0.10 times the maximum refined score are pruned, except for the S=10 strongest initial items, and at most L=5 unseen triples are materialized using Eq. (5). Retrieved graph facts are packed into a 7,000-token context. Full retrieval settings appear in Appendix C.Indexing follows Section 3.2 and uses Claude Haiku 4.5 for extraction and graph summarization. BGE-M3 (∼560M parameters) supplies all embeddings (Chen et al., 2024), and gpt-4o-mini generates the final answers for direct comparison with MAB Table 17.All ActionRAG experiments were run on a consumer Apple Silicon laptop (macOS 26.5.2, Darwin 25.5.0, arm64). In comparison, MAB reports HippoRAG-v2 timings on four NVIDIA L40 GPUs with an AMD EPYC 7713 CPU, so the latency results are not hardware-matched.

Figure 1: We present Agentic Hazard Mapper, a multi-agent system that emulates cartographic expertise to transform complex hazard maps into clearer, more actionable representations for risk communication. By coordinating specialized AI agents across stages of the professional cartographic workflow, the system emulates the iterative reasoning and design trade-offs of expert map-making, particularly in contexts where cartographic expertise is limited. Abstract Hazard maps are essential tools for public risk communication, preparedness, and evacuation planning, yet effective cartographic design is not always ensured due to limited access to cartographic expertise across local governments and communities. We present Agentic Hazard Mapper, a multi-agent system that automates hazardmap production by emulating professional cartographic workflows and iterative design trade-offs while adapting design decisions to different data, locations, and hazard contexts. We conducted a formative study with map experts to inform the system design, followed by a user study and interviews with map experts and hazard practitioners. The generated maps improved participants’ spatial understanding and evacuation-planning performance, reduced perceived workload and task completion time, and were generally preferred over corresponding municipal maps. We further discuss human oversight, adaptation across users and communication contexts, and opportunities to extend agentic support across broader stages of hazard-map production and risk communication. Keywords hazard maps, risk communication, agentic AI, multi-agent systems, map design 1 Introduction Natural hazards can cause substantial loss of life, damage to infrastructure, and disruption to communities. Japan is particularly susceptible to a wide range of natural hazards, including earthquakes, tsunamis, floods, and landslides, which occur across the country on a recurring basis [4]. In recent years, large-scale disasters have occurred, such as the 2016 Kumamoto Earthquake, Typhoon No. 14 in 2022, and heavy rainfalls caused by the Baiu Rainy Season Wu et al. Front in 2023. To mitigate the damage caused by natural hazards, effective risk communication is necessary for the general public to understand and prepare for the hazards. Hazard maps offer an important instrument for risk communication, as they present spatial information and intensity of potential hazards, which help people quickly gain knowledge about hazard extent, evacuation routes, and local terrain, compared to text-only messages [23, 25]. As such, hazard maps must ensure that the general public can understand and correctly interpret the presented information [25]. However, hazard-map production in Japan is decentralized across more than 1,700 municipalities, where the access to professional cartographic expertise can be limited or uneven, leaving many design decisions to practitioners whose primary expertise lies in hazard analysis or disaster management rather than cartography and visualization. This results in considerable variation in map design and generally limited attention to cartographic representation [26]. Such variation can substantially affect how people interpret hazard information and, in some cases, increase the likelihood of misinterpretation [27]. This gap is also reflected in residents’ experiences with hazard maps. According to a nationwide survey conducted in 2021, only 23.2% of respondents who had viewed their municipal hazard map considered it very useful for evacuation planning, while 56.4% considered it somewhat useful [30]. Respondents who found the maps less useful reported difficulties in map reading such as identifying the type and severity of hazards affecting their homes, deciding on the evacuation destination, and determining which evacuation routes to take. These responses highlight persistent challenges in translating technical hazard information into visual representations that support effective risk communication. Addressing these challenges calls for an automated system that can incorporate cartographic expertise in contexts where such expertise is limited. At the same time, rather than applying a single uniform design standard, such a system should remain flexible enough to make context-dependent adaptations, as data availability, hazard characteristics, geographic conditions, and local communication needs vary considerably across municipalities. These requirements are difficult to capture in a static workflow, where design decisions are predefined. Recent advances in AI provide new opportunities for supporting this type of adaptive reasoning. Agentic AI is particularly promising because it can address more open-ended and context-sensitive problems beyond narrow, well-defined tasks. Such systems coordinate specialized large language model (LLM) agents, decompose complex tasks into multiple stages, dynamically adapt strategies to changing conditions, and iteratively refine their decisions based on intermediate results and feedback [6, 10, 40]. These capabilities make agentic systems well suited to hazard map-making. In this paper, we propose an agentic system for automatically producing hazard maps for effective risk communication. We focus on printed maps, as they remain one of the most widely used media for hazard communication in Japan. The system is designed to iteratively refine map quality, adapt to different data, locations, and hazard characteristics, and remain grounded in established cartographic practices, rules, and preferences. We use insights from a formative study with map experts to inform the system design, and then conduct a user study as well as expert interviews to investigate how the cartographic expertise is operationized through the system, how the resulting maps are perceived, and how such a system could be used in actual hazard-preparedness contexts. To summarize, our contributions are: • We conducted a formative study with map experts to characterize expert map-making practices, including explicit cartographic guidelines and tacit design preferences for effective visual communication, and used these insights to inform the design of our agentic system. • We designed and implemented an agentic map-making system that incorporates expert cartographic knowledge and practices to automatically generate hazard maps, with the goal of supporting map production in contexts where cartographic expertise is limited or unavailable. • We conducted a user study to evaluate how effectively the generated maps support spatial understanding, risk comprehension, and evacuation planning. • We conducted interviews with map experts and hazard practitioners to assess the cartographic quality and practical utility of the generated maps, and to identify opportunities and challenges for integrating agentic map-making systems into real-world hazard-preparedness workflows. 2 Related work 2.1 Risk communication and hazard maps Broadly speaking, there are two types of hazard risk communication: warnings of incoming threats and communicating long-term risks for early preparedness and mitigation [39]. For the latter, maps have long been recognized for pre-disaster preparation and evacuation route planning [23]. However, the visual communication of maps is not always effective. For example, for the case of hurricane forecasting maps, the general public can sometimes struggle with interpreting geographic risk areas or uncertainty levels [3]. More generally, substantial variation exists in how people comprehend hazard maps and draw appropriate conclusions from the spatial information presented [22]. Recent reviews [48] continued to highlight challenges related to readability, visual complexity, color conventions, and risk perception. The effective visual design of hazard maps has long been studied in cartography and risk communication. Prior work [28] has examined how flood-risk communication through maps can increase awareness and support preparedness. Other works have investigated how hazard information can be represented with an appropriate balance between simplicity and complexity [13], how cartographic variables such as color, symbols, size, typography, and basemap styles influence the readability and interpretation of flood and evacuation maps [12, 21, 27, 41]. Works like [21, 34] have investigated cartographic recommendations and explicit design criteria for effective risk communication for flood and seismic hazards. Rather than a uniform design scheme, Meyer et al. [29] proposed user-specific adaptations in map content and visualization. Beyond visual design, Koesten et al. [20] showed that crisis-map interpretation can also be hindered by insufficient explanatory information, limited personal relevance, and distrust in the visualization. Together, these studies provide an established body of cartographic knowledge for hazard maps and inspire the design of our system. Agentic Hazard Mapper: Emulating Expert Map-Making with AI Agents for Risk Communication Communication of imminent hazards, in contrast, often extends beyond maps alone and combines textual warnings, alerts, visual information, and other modalities to support timely protective action [23]. Prior work has examined how emergency organizations communicate with the public through online and social-media channels during emerging disasters [17], as well as how technologies can support professionals in authoring effective severe-weather risk messages [18]. Such warning scenarios involve rapidly changing conditions, greater temporal pressure, and immediate protective actions. In this work, we focus primarily on map-based communication for longer-term hazard preparedness and evacuation planning, where cartographic design can support spatial understanding and planning before an emergency unfolds. 2.2 LLMs and agentic systems for automated visualization Automating visualization design has long been a goal of the visualization community. Traditional approaches typically formalize visualization knowledge as explicit rules, design guidelines, or optimization constraints, such as Voyager [45], Draco [31], and VizML [16]. While these approaches can produce effective visualizations, they often rely on predefined design spaces and are less flexible in handling complex natural-language requests, ambiguous user intentions, and diverse data characteristics. Recent advances in generative AI have enabled a new paradigm for automated visualization. Early approaches such as Data2Vis [9] learned visualization specifications from a given dataset, which are later transformed to visualization plots. More recently, LLMs have extended this paradigm by interpreting natural-language requests, reasoning about visualization choices, and generating executable visualization code. They been applied to various visualization tasks, including visualization recommendation and design assistance [36, 44], visualization code generation [5, 50], and visualization evaluation and critique [37]. Compared with traditional rule-based systems, LLMs provide greater flexibility in interpreting user requests and synthesizing visualization designs from heterogeneous sources of knowledge. Beyond visualization, LLM-based agents have demonstrated the ability to perform complex planning and decision-making tasks in open-ended environments. For example, [43] introduced an embodied LLM agent for Minecraft that continuously acquires skills, interacts with the environment, and accumulates knowledge through iterative exploration. More recently, researchers have explored multi-agent systems in which multiple specialized LLM agents collaborate to solve complex tasks. Such systems have been applied to code generation [15], software engineering [32], and general-purpose agent frameworks [46]. Rather than relying on a single model, multi-agent systems decompose problems into specialized subtasks and coordinate the reasoning processes of multiple agents, often leading to improved robustness, planning, and error recovery. Within visualization research, several agentic systems have recently emerged such as MatPlotAgent [47], CoDA [6], and VisPath [35]. Given user requirements in natural language and input datasets, these systems can analyze tasks, select visualization strategies, generate executable code, verify outputs, and iteratively refine results. For example, CoDA [6] adopts a collaborative multi-agent architecture consisting of specialized agents for metadata analysis, task planning, code generation, debugging, and self-reflection. Our agentic map-generation system can be situated within the broader landscape of LLM-powered visualization and multi-agent systems. 2.3 AI-assisted map-making Early AI-assisted map-making primarily explored map generation and style transfer through image synthesis. These approaches include GAN-based methods [7, 19], diffusion-based generation [1], and direct use of off-the-shelf models such as DALL·E [8, 11]. Although these methods can produce visually compelling results, pixel-based generation may introduce hallucinated or geographically inaccurate content and offers limited flexibility and finegrained control over cartographic elements during map generation. More recently, LLMs have been integrated with GIS and cartographic tools to support more structured map-making workflows. MapGPT [49] uses an LLM to interpret natural-language mapping requirements, decompose user requests into subtasks, and invoke specialized cartographic tools to manipulate individual map elements. By grounding the generation process in structured geographic data and tool-based operations, MapGPT provides greater control over map content and reduces the risk of geographic hallucinations. While MapGPT uses a single, centralized agent for map generation, CartoAgent [42] employs a multi-agent framework for map styling and restyling, consisting of preparation, design, and evaluation agents. The preparation agent extracts style information, such as color palettes, from user-provided reference maps; the design agent proposes color schemes and map symbols; and the evaluation agent assesses whether the generated map is visually effective and informative. The design is iteratively revised until it satisfies the evaluation criteria. Its workflow is mainly structured as a staged pipeline for map styling and evaluation, with limited emphasis on persistent memory, targeted reflection, or richer inter-agent collaboration across the broader cartographic workflow. Building on this trajectory, our system models a broader cartographic cycle spanning data processing, design and layout, evaluation, and revision, with specialized agents grounded in cartographic knowledge, practices, and expert preferences. 3 Formative Study To understand professional map-making practices and the challenges surrounding current hazard-map visualization in Japan, we conducted a formative study with map experts. We focused on how experts approach the map-making process, the cartographic principles and constraints that guide their decisions, the challenges they perceive in existing hazard maps, and the evaluation criteria to assess the map quality, in the context of hazard mapping and risk communication. The goal of the study was to elicit both explicit design knowledge and tacit professional judgments that could inform the design of our agentic hazard-mapping system. 3.1 Method We first reviewed literature on cartographic design, with particular attention to hazard mapping and risk communication. From the literature [12, 13, 21, 24, 27, 33, 34, 38, 48], we extracted a set of Wu et al. fundamental cartographic principles and identified 16 criteria describing what an effective hazard map should achieve and how they could be operationalized through cartographic variables such as hue, lightness, symbol size, line style, texture, and layer order. Requirements prescribed by official hazard-mapping guidelines were treated separately as fixed constraints. We recruited five experts (E1–E5) with between 3 and 40 years of professional experience in cartography, including two with particular expertise in hazard visualization. During structured, on-site interviews, experts first described their typical cartographic workflows. They then assessed three existing Japanese hazard maps with respect to cartographic principles, risk communication, and opportunities for improvement. Finally, experts evaluated the 16 literature-derived criteria, ranked their importance, selected the eight they considered most critical, and explained their choices. Afterward, they discussed how the design variables of these criteria should be adapted to different hazard types, data complexity, geographic characteristics, and communication needs. 3.2 Insights and findings Cartographic Workflow Experts described map-making as an iterative rather than linear process. A typical cartographic workflow starts by deciding determining the map’s purposes and intended audience, followed by collecting and checking data, selecting relevant information, and establishing a visual hierarchy to decide what important features stand out from the background. Cartographers then design colors, symbols, labels, and layout, scrutinize the result for mistakes or confusing details, and revise their earlier decisions as needed before publication. Problems in Current Hazard Maps The experts identified five main issues in current hazard maps: 1) Information overload. All experts noted that hazard maps often retain excessive geographic detail, including dense roads, buildings, labels, and contextual features that are not always relevant to the communicated hazard. Such information can compete with critical risk information and reduce readability. Experts also noted overly detailed classifications (E1, E2, E4) or legends containing unnecessary or unused categories (E3), which can increase users’ interpretive burden: 2) Weak visual hierarchy and confusing visual encoding. E3 and E5 observed that hazard-related information is not always visually distinguished from basemap information used primarily for orientation and context. They also noted confusing visual encoding: multiple hues within the same hazard type can make it difficult to perceive the ordering of severity levels, while similar colors or fill patterns across hazard types can make different hazards difficult to distinguish. 3) Limited interpretability of legends and symbols. E1, E2, and E3 noted that legends often lack clear structure and provide limited explanation. Rather than relying heavily on extensive legends, E3, E4, and E5 suggested using more intuitive color schemes and self-explanatory symbols can provoke users’ existing visual associations and reduce the need for repeated legend consultation. 4) Insufficient emphasis on meaningful labels. E4 and E5 emphasized the importance of labels for shelters, communities, landmarks, and other recognizable locations that help residents orient themselves and plan evacuation routes. Such information should be selectively emphasized rather than treated as equivalent to less relevant geographic annotations. 5) Inadequate representation of topography and elevation. Most experts (E1, E3, E4, and E5) emphasized the importance of terrain and elevation particularly for floods and landslides. However, this information is either absent or difficult to interpret in existing maps. For example, conventional contour lines can convey precise elevation information but may be less intuitive for the general public. Experts also identified useful existing practices. E1, E2, and E3 valued illustrations linking flood-inundation depths to affected building storeys, as they make abstract depth values easier to interpret. E2 and E4 also noted that historical hazard information can strengthen risk awareness by connecting risks to past experience, although it is less useful for assessing current conditions. Aspects for Effective Risk Communication Across the interviews, four broader communication goals emerged. First, hazard maps should support risk awareness by making affected areas and relative severity readily perceivable (E1–E5). Second, they should support spatial awareness by helping users identify shelters, neighborhoods, roads, terrain, and potential evacuation routes (E1–E5). Third, maps should establish personal relevance, allowing users to understand how hazards may affect their own circumstances and possible actions (E1–E5). Finally, E3 and E5 emphasized multihazard awareness, to distinguish and associate hazards that overlap spatially or interact in ways relevant to evacuation decisions. Quality criteria for hazard map design Experts prioritized eight criteria for guiding design and evaluation: information density, hazard differentiation, visual hierarchy, symbol interpretability, basemap clarity, orientation and localizability, label readability, and legend clarity. Information density received particularly strong emphasis, with all experts advocating the simplification or removal of less relevant information when it competes with hazard-related content. Experts also emphasized clear differentiation between hazard types and severity levels through appropriate color encoding and intuitive symbols. They also emphasized a strong visual hierarchy that can be established through variables such as size, font, color, and transparency. At the same time, basemap information should remain sufficiently legible to support orientation, particularly major roads and topographic features. Labels important for localization and evacuation, such as shelter names, community names, landmarks, and facility names, should remain identifiable and unobscured by competing visual elements. Finally, legends should be concise, clearly organized, and use plain-language descriptions where possible. By contrast, criteria related primarily to aesthetics and color harmony received lower priority. We derived weights for each criterion based on how many experts have voted for this. Importantly, experts stressed that these criteria cannot be applied through a single fixed design scheme. Their implementation depends on factors such as map scale, spatial extent, available data, terrain, and hazard characteristics. Design choices can also conflict with one another, requiring trade-offs and iterative adjustment. This makes flexible professional judgment central to effective hazard-map design. Agentic Hazard Mapper: Emulating Expert Map-Making with AI Agents for Risk Communication 3.3 Design implications Based on these findings, we made the following design decisions for our system: Risk-centered information organization and visual hierarchy. The system should organize and simplify information according to the communication goal, prioritizing content that directly supports risk understanding and evacuation planning while secondary information can be reduced or omitted when appropriate. This priority should also be reflected visually, with the dominant hazard visualization and still sufficiently legible contextual information to support orientation and localization. Adaptive and flexible approach. Rather than applying a uniform visual template, the system should adapt to hazard type and severity, available data, terrain, urban structure, map scale, and locally relevant landmarks or evacuation resources. Established criteria and expert heuristics should guide decisions without prescribing a single fixed solution, thereby preserving flexibility in selecting appropriate visual variables, parameters, and representations. Semantically and spatially grounded representation. Colors, symbols, labels, and other visual variables should preserve clear semantic distinctions between hazard types, severity levels, and contextual information. At the same time, maps should preserve meaningful spatial anchors for orientation and localization, and provide interpretable terrain information when topography is relevant to risk understanding. Oat is trained only on successful trajectories and pinpoints which steps of a failed trajectory caused the failure, with no labels. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026.

Nine benchmarks, not two or three. Epoch AI ran its Benchmark Reviews program across 15 widely cited tests and could only fully verify four of them: ExploitBench v0.1, SimpleQA Verified, PostTrainBench v1.1, and WeirdML v2. Nine others, including SWE-bench Verified, SWE-Bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 4.0.0, Humanity's Last Exam, and HealthBench Professional, got flagged flawed. Two more came back inconclusive.

The bar for flawed is an error rate of 20% or higher in a stratified sample of 50 tasks, or a grading problem systemic enough that sample size stops mattering. The errors aren't typos. Reviewers found invalid tasks, false negatives, false positives, under-elicitation, setup bias, and silent versioning, where a benchmark quietly changed underneath the leaderboard. A separate citation in the same review found errors in 42% of FrontierMath v1 problems.

SWE-bench Verified making that list matters more than the others because it's the single most quoted number in coding-agent marketing right now, the same leaderboard every CLI and IDE agent cites to prove itself. Hamel Husain, who has spent his career building evals, called the gap between benchmark quality and industry reliance on them astounding, and he's not alone in paying to close it. Braintrust raised a 36 million dollar Series A led by a16z at a 150 million dollar valuation this year, with Notion, Stripe, Airtable, and Zapier among the customers paying between five figures and over 100,000 dollars to run their own evals instead of trusting a published score. Braintrust's own numbers claim accuracy often climbs from under 40% to over 80% within weeks of adopting real evaluation.

A leaderboard number is marketing until someone runs the failed examples by hand. Most teams still skip that step because the benchmark did the work of looking rigorous for them.
